groups.title: Listening
groups.instructions: You are going to listen to a woman interviewing a student about eating habits. Read each question and choose the correct answer. You have 1 minute and 30 seconds to look through the questions before you listen. You will listen to the passage twice only, so listen carefully. /6 x 2 = 12 points/
groups.context:
Woman: Hello. I'm from the health centre, and we're doing a survey about students' eating habits. Can I ask you some questions?
Boy: Sure.
Woman: What's your name?
Boy: David Harper. That's H-A-R-P-E-R.
Woman: Thank you, David. Do you usually eat breakfast?
Boy: Not really. I used to have breakfast every day, but now I get up late, so I usually just have a glass of milk.
Woman: And what about lunch?
Boy: I eat in the school canteen. The food is OK, but I'd like more salads.
Woman: How often do you eat fast food?
Boy: About twice a month, usually after football matches with my team. Last year it was every weekend, but my coach told us it's bad for our fitness.
Woman: Do you cook?
Boy: Yes, I cook dinner for my family on Fridays. My speciality is fried rice!
Woman: That's great. One last question: what are you doing after this?
Boy: I'm going to the supermarket. I need to buy vegetables for tonight's dinner.

passages.title: Passage 1
passages.text:
Most teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep every night, but research shows that many get far less. There are several reasons for this. Homework and after-school activities take up a lot of time, and many young people use their phones in bed late at night.

Scientists have also discovered that teenagers' body clocks are different from those of children and adults. During the teenage years, the body starts producing the sleep hormone melatonin later in the evening. As a result, teenagers often do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or later, but **they** still have to get up early for school.

Lack of sleep can cause serious problems. Tired students find it harder to concentrate and remember information, and they are more likely to feel stressed or have accidents. For this reason, some schools in the United States have started classes later in the morning. The results have been <u>encouraging</u>: students' grades and attendance have improved.
